title: Tau's provider/tool agent loop
question: How does Tau turn one user question into model calls, tool calls, and follow-up turns?
teleprompter_points: The direct answer: tau_agent.loop.run_agent_loop is the pure loop; AgentHarness owns session state around it.
The provider streams neutral events; the loop turns them into Tau agent events.
When the model asks for tools, Tau executes them, appends tool-result messages, then calls the provider again.
Steering and follow-up messages are late-injected only between turns, not hidden inside tools.
proof_boundary: Explains Tau's in-process portable agent loop, not provider quality or UI rendering.

debugger_stops.proves: The loop receives provider, transcript, and tools as injected dependencies.
A tool call is executed before the next model turn.

related_questions: What is the provider boundary?

title: Provider-neutral model streaming boundary
question: Where does Tau isolate model providers from the agent loop?
teleprompter_points: The direct answer: ModelProvider is the small protocol between tau_agent and tau_ai.
Providers stream ProviderEvent objects; the agent loop does not know the SDK shape.
OpenAI, Anthropic, SciLLM, and FakeProvider can all satisfy the same boundary.
This is why Tau can test the loop with FakeProvider without live model calls.
proof_boundary: Explains the Python protocol boundary, not any provider's external SLA.

title: Canonical DAG runtime flow
question: How does Tau execute a public DAG contract durably?
teleprompter_points: The direct answer: public contracts compile to DagPlan, then run_dag_plan drives node execution and journals transitions in DagRunStore.
DagPlan is the frozen backend-neutral shape.
The scheduler decides readiness, executes nodes, validates results, and commits transition batches.
Replay rebuilds state from committed journal records instead of trusting live memory.

Preflight happens before any provider or tool runs.
Only read-only tools are allowed in the native reviewer path covered here.
Settlement is mapped back to a scheduler attempt result.

Runtime requirements, source bindings, security declarations, and profile defaults are frozen into the plan.
The resulting DagPlan hash is the identity later checked by scheduler, replay, and viewer code.

title: Scheduler authority and transition policy
question: Who decides that a Tau DAG node is ready, retried, joined, blocked, or terminal?
teleprompter_points: The direct answer: run_dag_plan owns readiness, attempts, transition batches, and terminal settlement.
Adapters and providers can produce observations; they cannot authorize successors by themselves.
Transition policy validates node completions, edge settlement, cancellation, deadlines, and blocks.
The scheduler commits accepted changes through the run store so replay can rebuild the same authority state.
proof_boundary: Explains scheduler policy authority, not whether an external worker behaves well.

title: Journal durability and crash recovery
question: What happens if Tau crashes after work produced evidence but before that evidence became authoritative?
teleprompter_points: The direct answer: Tau writes durable JSON/intents, stages results, commits journal records, then replay/reconciliation rebuilds state after interruption.
Durable writes are read back before trust.
Startup reconciliation quarantines or settles incomplete artifacts instead of silently accepting them.
Replay reconstructs scheduler state from committed records, not from live process memory.
proof_boundary: Explains local durability and recovery mechanics, not hardware-level filesystem guarantees beyond fsync/readback.

title: Runtime backend authority boundary

The registry selects an implementation by capability; it does not change DAG policy.
RuntimeEventBridge normalizes observations before they become durable scheduler evidence.
